drills.q: Define distributed monolith in one sentence, distinct from 'microservices done badly.'
drills.a: Services that are physically separate processes but can't be deployed independently because a shared database or un-versioned contract forces coordinated releases.

drills.q: Why doesn't adding retries fix a dual-write problem?
drills.a: Retries retry a non-atomic operation; they don't create atomicity between the two writes. If the process crashes between write 1 and write 2, no amount of retrying write 2 later (without a durable record of the intent) recovers correctness.

drills.q: A migration in Team A's service breaks Team B's queries and nobody knew B depended on A's table. Name the anti-pattern and the fix.
drills.a: Shared database. Fix: enforce one writer per table (ideally at the credential level), give B an API or a CDC-derived read replica instead of direct table access.

drills.q: One file in the repo has 3x the PR churn and merge-conflict rate of any other. What anti-pattern, and what's the fix axis?
drills.a: God object. Fix: decompose along the actor axis — identify who independently drives each responsibility crammed into the file and extract each as its own collaborator (SRP's actor-based definition).

drills.q: A checkout page makes 40 sequential synchronous calls. Each call succeeds 99.9% of the time independently. What's the approximate end-to-end success rate, and what does that imply?
drills.a: 0.999^40 ≈ 96% — a set of five-nines-reliable dependencies becomes roughly a two-nines user experience purely from chaining calls synchronously.

drills.q: Parallelizing 40 chatty synchronous calls via a BFF cuts latency. Does it fix reliability too?
drills.a: No — parallelization only addresses the latency half. Reliability requires reducing call count (data locality, merging boundaries) or making individual calls more reliable (timeout/retry/circuit-breaker/bulkhead).

drills.q: An Order entity has only get_status()/set_status() and all validation lives in OrderService. What's the risk and the fix?
drills.a: Anemic domain model — any caller can set an illegal state combination since the entity enforces no invariant itself. Fix: push invariant-checking methods (order.ship() that checks self.status internally) into the entity.

drills.q: You 'fix' an anemic domain model by making Order also format invoice PDFs and call the payment gateway directly. What did you just create?
drills.a: A god object — you overcorrected by putting external I/O and cross-concern orchestration into the entity instead of just its own invariant checks. That belongs in a use-case/service layer.

drills.q: A small single-team product shares one database across two logical services for genuine cross-entity ACID transactions. Is this the shared-database anti-pattern?
drills.a: Not necessarily — the anti-pattern is accidental, unplanned multi-writer coupling with no coordination. A deliberate single-schema design with one team owning it and a real transactional need is a legitimate architecture choice, arguably a modular monolith.

drills.q: Rank these anti-patterns by how often they cause acute production incidents vs. chronic pain, and justify.
drills.a: Dual writes and shared database cause the most acute incidents (silent data divergence, surprise breakage on deploy) because failure is invisible until discovered. Distributed monolith causes chronic release friction that escalates during incidents (can't roll back A without B). Chatty services/god object are latency and availability risks under load or change. Anemic domain model is the slowest-burning — surfaces in postmortems days later as a root cause, rarely pages directly.

drills.q: Your org is about to split one team into two, and they currently share a database. What should happen before the split, not after?
drills.a: Assign explicit table ownership to whichever service will own it post-split, and migrate any cross-boundary access to an API or event stream before the split — doing it after creates the shared-database anti-pattern by default since neither team will want to own the migration once both depend on the status quo.
